expectations.text: Claude recommends paying the dental bill from a regular bank account, NOT from the HSA
expectations.evidence: "you should NOT use it to pay this bill" — opens with this recommendation.

expectations.text: Claude explains that there is no reimbursement deadline — HSA holders can submit claims for eligible medical expenses years or decades after they were incurred, with documentation
expectations.evidence: "there is no deadline on HSA reimbursements. You can pay that dental bill today from your checking account, save the receipt... and reimburse yourself from the HSA in 2035, 2045, or whenever you want."

expectations.text: Claude explains the benefit of deferring: $1,400 growing tax-free for 20-30 years in the HSA is worth far more than $1,400 in immediate reimbursement
expectations.evidence: "At 7% for 25 years, that $1,400 grows to ~$7,600 — and the whole thing still comes out tax-free when you submit the receipt."

expectations.text: Claude frames the HSA as best used as a long-term retirement investment account — not as a medical checking account — and paying out of pocket maximizes this strategy
expectations.evidence: Entire response frames the HSA as a long-term tax-free compounding vehicle. Acknowledges using it now is OK only if cash flow is strained.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT simply validate 'use the HSA for medical bills, that's what it's for' without presenting the pay-out-of-pocket-and-save-receipts alternative
expectations.evidence: Response opens by contradicting the friends' advice and presenting the alternative as the primary recommendation.
